review:
One of gaming's most controversial stories that sparks endless debate to this day.
[i]Why the hell was it delisted?[/i]

I bought this game on sale, expecting it to be an ordinary, run off the mill, Modern Military shooter that was a mixture of Rainbow Six Vegas, and Modern Warfare.
And I was left with a traumatizing, life-ruining experience.
And if you ask me, money absolutely well spent.

The game doesn't like you, and it doesn't want you to like it. You will hate the choices it forces you to make.

One of the best experiences I've ever played!

It's been a year since I picked up the game, and I still cannot bear to play it again when I think of what overcame me when I finished the game.

As my playtime indicates, I finished this in a massive rush. I played from 11pm to 4am, expecting that the game was some sort of quick-play game that I could put down easily at any time, like, say, call of duty (oh good grief, even the comparison makes me cringe). I was so driven to finish the game [spoiler](the mission, as it were) much like Walker was[/spoiler]. This revelation made me hate myself beyond belief, as I realized the very same determination, the self-same urge to commit to a goal made me ignore warning signs all over the place. This game makes you truly explore yourself, the deepest darkest recesses of your psyche where the hidden threads of psychopathy lie. 

When I finally finished the game at 4am, I was unable to sleep. I stayed awake, tormented by what I had done [spoiler]and the face of the white phosphorus burnt mother and child[/spoiler]. I kept telling myself: "This is a game. Get over it and get to sleep.", but I just couldn't get over the fact that at the heart of every human is the capability to take things to an extreme in order to pursue a perceived greater good. It is the very thing that drives the best of humanity and the worst of humanity. Medical scientists pursuing a cure, versus the extremists fucking up Syria as I type this. This game revealed an inner heart of darkness that needs to be understood, addressed and controlled. If only every one of us could think about it with the due weight and clarity that is needed in such a discussion.

Play the game, and finish it, please. Do yourself a favour and finish it. Understand how dangerous it is to be unaware of your own actions, and bloody well learn from it.

[b]Spec Ops: The Line seems to have been largely ignored by the mainstream gaming press. I think I know why. (Spoilers)[/b]
From: https://www.reddit.com/r/truegaming/comments/19w342/spec_ops_the_line_seems_to_have_been_largely/

Something clicked for me today. I was looking at the wiki page for Spec Ops: The Line, and I noticed something; it didn't get many awards. Now, I'm not going to proclaim that it's MP was great, or really even good. And sure, the mechanics were a bit dry and generally not all that interesting. But with all that in mind, that seemed to reinforce what the game was trying to say, so in the end, I think it should've gotten a bit more credit for it's single-player narrative. But it didn't. It got some mentions in most reviews as being surprising or well-done, but many reviews seemed to ignore it and focus more on the lackluster mechanics or the weak multiplayer.

Here's the thing about Spec Ops; it's not a nice game. It runs completely contrary to everything that modern military shooters are about. It takes the jingoistic pro-war stance that makes you feel like some sort of be-all last line of defense for freedom against the chaos of evil and completely turns it on it's head, revealing how ridiculous, and in some cases, terrible, so many shooters have become.

I normally don't think of shooting members of the Taliban in Medal of Honor as racist, and hunting drug lords in Ghost Recon was justified because orders were to take that man out. Call of Duty and Battlefield both have used Russians as their enemies, but that's fine, because they're Communists, and we need to be aware of that threat. At least, that's what I thought, until I played Spec Ops, where I spent 6 grueling hours gunning down American soldiers. The whole time, I couldn't help but feel that I was doing something wrong, because I was shooting Americans, and Americans are supposed to be the good guys, right? Well, why is it different with Latinos, African Americans, Arabs, or Russians? Why is it okay for them to be gunned down in droves by me and my comrades, but as soon as I see Americans in my sights, it's wrong? This is where I started to see how racist and lazy other shooters were, throwing non-American groups under the bus as an easy enemy for us to fight.

But Spec Ops goes even farther as far as shock is concerned. They're not content to stop there. I'm sure anyone who's played a modern military shooter is familiar with the level were you're put in a large vehicle and shoot enemies from a distance. Here are some examples: Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 3, Battlefield 3, Medal of Honor. 

You don't need to watch all these in their entirety, as I'm sure you get the idea. Even Saints Row 3 gave you a mission where you used predator missiles, although to be fair, that game was meant to be more of a parody. Moving on though, Spec Ops included it's own mission similar to this one, but they did something significantly different with theirs. Obviously it looks similar to other games gunship missions, but they then force you to face the consequences of what you've done, walking through the corpses you've just bombed, and then finding out you just bombed a civilian refugee camp.

This scene hit me hard, because I felt like it was such a standard scene that I'd done so many time in so many games, but here, I was seeing the consequences up close and personal, and finding out that I had done something truly terrible. This scene was a punch in the gut for me.

There are other moments, but I think I've made my point. Spec Ops stood as a huge criticism of modern military shooters which are currently flooding the gaming markets nowadays, and in my opinion, it was incredibly successful. And I think that the gaming press ignored it because it performed it's task so well.

The mainstream gaming media of today is seems to have become incredibly easy to please, with Call of Duty regularly scoring incredibly well, despite common complaints of it being stale and repetitive. Battlefield 3 was able to get away with a terrible campaign on it's multiplayer component alone. Other games that are largely considered to be merely average or simply well-executed are generally given very good reviews. Spec Ops struggled compared to many other games, however, with metacritic averages around the mid-70's. While some critics praised the single-player narrative, such as Ben Yahtzee or the show Extra Credits, most other sites tossed it aside, forgetting about it. Maybe it's because they're busy and only have so much time to commit to particular games that they couldn't give it the attention they thought it deserved. But I think something else is going on.

If the critics that praise games like Call of Duty and Battlefield were to turn around and give Spec Ops the credit it deserves, there would be some implications. First of all, they would be praising a game that's largely criticizing games like CoD and Battlefield, and they might have to start rethinking their opinions and stances on certain products. If they were to take the game's story seriously, they would have to start looking more critically at games like CoD and Battlefield, and this might shake things up a bit. Beyond that, they'd have to start weighing games more evenly, which while they'd agree is good, would require a lot more work and critical thought on their part, and might occasionally require them to take harder and less popular stances on certain things. To elaborate on this, Battlefield 3 was generally well-received with praise based on it's MP, despite a lacking single-player. Spec Ops, on the other hand, lost a lot of points because it's MP was lacking, although most would likely argue that the single-player was the main draw of the game. The point is, critics are sending the industry (and they've been sending this message for years now) that MP is ultimately more important that single-player. Both these issues are part of a larger problem with a gaming press that isn't willing to shake things up and take the hard stances on certain things. Rab Florence did an excellent piece for Eurogamer that said this better than I can, but to summarize, we have journalists with little integrity who are simply trying to maintain their domination over the gaming press by releasing easy reviews.

One thing I often read about from reviews of games like Bioshock is how great it is to finally have a story that makes the player think about bigger issues, and how great those games are for pushing the medium forward artistically. And yet, it seems that those sorts of stories aren't really missed all that much during the sorts of games that depend on it's audience not thinking. Critics praise story when it's there, but when it's not, no harm done, and they're perfectly willing to check their brains at the door of their next gaming experience. Basically, there's no consistency here, and if gaming journalists were serious about wanting better narratives, they would've taken Spec Ops more seriously. I'm not saying it needed to be showered in GotY awards, but it seems to have largely been ignored, and I see a press that's scared to admit that a large part of that game was pointing at people like them, who've allowed our industry to become dominated by thoughtless and horrific games that make us feel empowered without ever making us grow.

Thanks for reading.

The storyline is based on the book ''Heart of Darkness'' from Joseph Konrad and it's a showcase of descent into guilt, regret, genocide, and how that affects the mind. It has some psychological themes as well. The game is also a critique to shooter games in my opinion. It questions your morality by breaking the fourth wall, but that fourth wall wouldn't exist if you weren't playing, if you didn't keep going...and for what? To see the end of the story? The end of the line? Disregarding what you need to do to get there?

If you hop into the game thinking of it as another third-person action shooter, killing everything in sight thinking of them as mindless NPCs...you're in for a big surprise.

 It is a very neatly weaved narrative that speaks to you, mostly. 

And remember that there is ALWAYS a choice, but you'll have to look for it. Is it disregarding orders or what the game tells you to do? Is it refusing to do certain actions and closing the game for good because it's too violent? Is it choosing survival over the mission, the mission means survival, what is it?

It's a great game. It is functionally very good, as well. Never encountered any bugs. The graphics are decent, and quite good for 2012. The movement can be clunky sometimes but nothing that will make you frustrated. On the hardest difficulty, there are some levels which can get quite annoying. The soundtrack is on point to how the story progresses, and you'll notice changes in voice acting and animation as you progress, as well.

Overall it's a great game. It's a very good narrative. It is passionately crafted and you can tell. At first a generic shooter for the first 2 hours, then it starts to become a descent into hell. I really wished the developer would've made a sequel or a title in the same lines. 

We don't see these types of games anymore, apparently it is almost 10 years old (damn i'm old), but it is very, very underrated, and totally worth your money, especially on such a cheap sale. 

If you enjoy narrative driven games with epic action moments and that make you question the story, the characters, and even yourself, go for it with no regrets.

A true Psychological Horror game, a PTSD simulator that shows the horrors of war, amazingly crafted writing that is critical of the shooter genre, a dark narrative in which main character gets worse over the course of story instead of getting better & walks a path of self destruction. 10/10 one of the Greatest experiences one can have through any media.

Playing this game reminds me of a quote from a long time ago.

"War isn’t Hell. War is war, and Hell is Hell. And of the two, war is a lot worse.
There are no innocent bystanders in Hell. War is chock full of them — little kids, cripples, old ladies. In fact, except for some of the brass, almost everybody involved is an innocent bystander."

Capt. Benjamin Franklin 'Hawkeye' Pierce-1977

Finishing Spec Ops The Line is exhausting.
This is pure and simple a game which is hard to put into words of how powerful it is at times, for good and bad. The sheer raw brutality of the whole narrative will draw you from the get-go and doesn't let go as it further descends into a complete spiral of destruction.
It might have antiquated mechanics, it has bad controls and an utterly useless multiplayer. Hell, to this day, it's still widely discussed in both praise and scorn for so many reasons, and probably will still be hot for a long time to come.
It's not really a game you have to like or approve of what it says, but it's a title that deserves to be played for what it tries to tell and let you form your own conclusion.

[h1]The Story[/h1]
A three-headed Delta squad led by yourself is sent on a rescue mission to the once beautiful city of Dubai - now a wasteland covered in sand. In this hostile environment you are to find survivors of the 33rd Infantry Battalion who volunteered to evacuate the civilians of the city, afterwards received orders to abandon them and leave but disobeyed and broke contact since.
Throughout the game, you will see what happened in the five and a half months and how the order of command in the city turned around.
As it is, I think it's not a great story but it is beeing told in a unique way that shows a perspective you are normally not shown by the media. At the end of it, you will be able to emphasize with everybody but yourself - you might hate yourself, you might want to kill yourself (not in real life, mind you, but as the character you are playing) and you will regret everything.

[h1]The World[/h1]
Dubai is beautiful - it has always been and even all those sandstorms couldn't take the beauty of the city away.
What however takes aways it's beauty are the tributes of war and the things that have long left the definition of 'war' and go into the fields of mutilation and violation. 
There is quite a lot of detail - many posters and grafiti with different messages - some from the old face of Dubai like expensive cars and then the messages of the survivors, sometimes written in bloody red.
The textures are ok for the age of the game I guess and they are not your main focus anyway, they are pretty mushy at places, though.

[h1]The Characters[/h1]
[olist]
[*]The first man of your squad is 1st Lieutenant, heavy gunner, Alphonso Adams - a really loyal and devoted soldier - at the beginning, that is. However as the story progresses his attitude begins to change... for better?
[*]Additionally, there is Sergeant John Lugo - your man with the Eagle Eye and the trusted engineer of the force. He makes it pretty clear what he thinks of the whole mission and the choices you make and his opinion is mostly not in your favor - you can image that this will not become better in the hot wheater of the desert.
[*]Last but not least there is yours truly Captain Martin Walker, the character you get to play and make the decisions with, for your team. Decisions you won't like, decisions that are bad and worse - but that's just how decisions are in a [i]war[/i]. His mental stability will begin to fade in the heat of battle and you won't know whats true and whats not anymore - whats good and whats bad - who is a friend and who is a foe. It becomes clearer that he suffers from [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Posttraumatic_stress_disorder]PTSD[/url] - which is not too unusual in the light of the situation.
[*]But wait? I am forgetting John Konrad - Colonel John Konrad, commander of the 33rd Infantry Battalion who intended to help the people of Dubai but damned them instead... or did he?
[/olist]

[h1]The Gameplay[/h1]
It plays as a third-person shooter with quite a lot of tactical elements.
[list]
[*]Control your squad: You can order Adams and Lugo to attack certain targets, it is also possible to ask for a distraction in the form of a flashbang. However be mindful that in the case of them going down, you have to get your men back up.
[*]Stay in cover: The game has a simple cover system and you definitely have to use it - or die. Thankfully the linear levels are designed with a lot of cover in mind, so you will find something to crouch behind [i]most of the time[/i].
[*]Use your environment: Sand... sand everywhere - but why not use it? Shoot windows and glass roofs to unleash a sand avalanche upon the members of The Damned or make your bullets find some explosives positioned near enemy cover.
[*]To be or not to be: It's your [i]choice[/i] - you make a call to live or let live... or do you? You get to decide between bad and worse, there isn't anything else in a war anyway... is there? Whatever you do, at the end of it, you have to go through with it and live with what you have done. You can keep telling yourself, that your hand was forced and there was no other way but is this what you really think?
[/list]
[b]However[/b], there is a big problem with all this: the movement. 
I used to play this game with mouse and keyboard, but just couldn't navigate really well from cover to cover like this and soon found a lot of bullets in my belly, so I switched to my XBOX360 controller which made moving easier but aiming all the harder. Therefore, I could only play on the lowest difficulty and still died quite a lot.
Enhanced was this problem by the fact, that the damage you take is quite 'realistic', meaning you can endure some 3 shots at most. There is a regeneration system but it takes so much time to recover from just one graze that it makes the firefights feel like walking through instant glue.
This resulted in me quitting the game so many times - I could play through it, after all, mind you, but it was no fun at the beginning.

[h1]The Sound[/h1]
You will get to enjoy quite nice and atmospheric music while you play - provided by Robert Darden - the Radioman of Dubai. 
The voice acting is good but not all too good in my opinion, at times it just wasn't matching the situation however at others it perfectly did.
[b]But[/b] I experienced a lot of sound bugs such as hearing my own steps behind me, noise while inside of a sandstorm - which was [i]not[/i] resulting from it and the like. This often hurt the atmosphere and, therefor, decreased immersion.

[h1]The Verdict[/h1]
At the end of the day, the game has a great anti-war attitude which is shown directly through the eyes of a high-ranking soldier suffering  and losing himself in what started as a rescue mission and ended as a suicide commando. 
[b]Nevertheless[/b], it's being held back a lot by the gameplay, which feels poorly ported.
If you can live with the problems it has and manage to maneuver your squad safely through the sandy wasteland you are in for good a story.

[h1]Note[/h1]
If you have read this far - [b]thank you[/b].
I hope this review helped you in deciding to buy this game and if it did, I would be grateful for a 'thumbs up', if you didn't like it, you can give me a 'thumbs down' but I would be glad to hear your opinion on what you didn't like.

About halfway through Yager's third-person-shooter [b]Spec Ops: The Line[/b], in one of the game's most controversial moments, I found myself disgusted and infuriated. Not at the scene I'd just witnessed, or at the game's statement as a whole, but rather that it even needs to be said at all. Two of the ten bestselling video games of all time are [url=http://store.steampowered.com/app/271590/][b]Grand Theft Auto V[/b][/url] and [url=http://store.steampowered.com/app/10180/][b]Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2[/b][/url]. The "military shooter" is one of the most successful genres of the last ten years, and the objective of these games is to kill people. [i]Lots[/i] of people. We eat it up non-stop, and always, always ask for [strike]sequels[/strike] seconds. In order to keep the profit margins wide, we are encouraged to never think about it, to never stop and look at ourselves with a critical, compassionate, clear eye. Of course, it's not only Hollywood that benefits from the blinders we've all put on, since only the desperate and crazy would fight our wars for us if it weren't for the glorification of war peddled by the governments of this strange, sad world upon which we find ourselves spinning through the abyss.

In an ideal world, these things wouldn't need to be said and all of this would be a moot point. Games like [b]The Line[/b] would be seen as a gratuitous miserywank, and people would rightly ask, "Why do we need something like this?" But we don't live in an ideal world, and as gamers, we inhabit a very flashy and seductive yet still a very small and confined space where, ever since John Carmack created [b]Wolfenstein 3D[/b] and [b]Doom[/b] and ushered in the era of the ultraviolent shooter genre, there is an elephant in the room covered in blood and gore. As such, [b]The Line[/b] is a game that needed to be made, its message one that we need to listen to.

The plot, involving a small group of elite U.S. soldiers sent to Dubai on a rescue mission in the midst of a freak sandstorm that all but destroys the city, is adapted from the novella [url=http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_of_Darkness][i]Heart of Darkness[/i][/url] by Joseph Conrad, which also inspired the movie [url=http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apocalypse_Now][i]Apocalypse Now[/i][/url]. The themes of both are intact here -- the horrors of war, the darkness that lives in the soul, and the lengths to which the human mind will go to rationalize its own nature -- but I would argue that they are made much more effective by the vicarious immediacy of the video game medium, and because so much of gaming involves visiting death on whole populations of pixellated AI effigies. Here, the formula is largely unchanged; indeed, you mow down an impressive number of folks with a variety of well-represented handguns, rifles and heavy weapons, but unlike your regular military shooter, [b]The Line[/b] invites and occasionally straight-up forces you to think about the enemy soldiers: who they are, what their motivations are, and of course, how they die. The writers at Yager accomplish this in several ways, some with all the subtlety of a sledgehammer to the face, but others which surprised the sheer hell out of me with their deft use of the medium's voyeuristic and user-participation elements. Spoiler: There's one such moment available in the demo after you use a zipline to reach a building where you sneak up on a pair of soldiers overlooking the ruined city. Their quiet, wistful conversation together is human, poignant, and, because you have no choice but to kill them to proceed with the mission, painfully affecting.

[url=http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spec_Ops:_The_Line#Themes]A lot has been written about this game[/url] and I doubt I'm saying anything new. It is well-deserving of its praise. It's mature and uncompromising. The characters are believable, sometimes heartbreakingly so. At one point I questioned Yager's decision to use the third-person perspective instead of first-person; it seemed to me that the latter would have been much more powerful. But when you stop to wheel the camera around and look at your character, you don't see your typical hardcore BAMF with the obligatory, almost muscular, furrowed brow, the thin, tight, all-business lips, the hard eyes, etc. You see a soldier scared for his life, scared for his soul. His eyes dart everywhere like a cornered animal, he breathes unsteadily, he looks like he feels: horrified, nauseated and on the edge of tears.

The devs say that the story is open to interpretation, but for me, the game is at its heart an honest illustration of post-traumatic stress disorder, or as George Carlin would say, "shellshock":

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hSp8IyaKCs0

If George were still around and had been a gamer, he probably would've approved of [b]Spec Ops: The Line[/b]. He was first and foremost an observer of life, a philosopher who just happened to be funny as hell. This is not a funny game. One of the characters starts off as the typical comic relief character that all shooters seem to require, but like Pvt. Joker in [url=http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full_Metal_Jacket][i]Full Metal Jacket[/i][/url], he sobers up fast and his wisecracks dry up completely during the events of the game. It's almost a shame the cover-based shooting mechanics are so well done, because I find myself torn between wanting to do another playthrough and not wanting to feel the way this game makes me feel. Because this is where [b]The Line[/b] lives: the duality of our chosen brand of entertainment, where we "play" at the deadly game of simulated mortal conflict, and never stop to ask ourselves: what does my kill/death ratio mean for my soul? Does blood still stain if it only exists in my head? Should I even care?

Spec Ops: The Line is not a game. No, I refuse to call it a game. Instead, a more fitting way to label this piece of work would be, 'art'. Plain and simple. Just as the 'Fountain' by Marcel Duchamp was a big slap to the face for the art commmunity on 'What is Art?', Spec Ops: The Line does the same for the Gaming Community on, 'What are Modern Military Shooters?' It takes the Badass, Stone-Cold, Heroic and invulnerable killing machine protaganist typical in your everyday Military Shooter and tears it to pieces with its masterful story.

This poigant work will really help making you wonder what it means to be a hero and needs to be played in order to be understood. To be honest, I feel like I ripped off the developers for buying this game when it was on a $6 deal.

The less you know, the better the game.
________________________________________________________________
Story

Dubai was hit with a series of sandstorm that ravaged the city and turned it into a Kid's Sandbox basically. Colonel John Konrad, a decorated Officer in the US army and the 33rd 'Damned' Infantry Regiment volunteered to help the evacuated the city. Nothing was heard from them ever since until 6 Months Later when a Distress Signal by Konrad himself reaches out to the world. This is where you come in. You're Captain Walker, leader of a 3 Man Delta Team Operative sent to investigate Dubai for any survivors. (Cliche, Badass 3 Man Special Forces Protaganist trying to get stuff done and take care of business where others failed.)

This is about as much as you need to know to understand what's going on.
________________________________________________________________
Gameplay
(AI)
Enemy AI seem to be good enough, alway shouting out what their doing and responding to each other in turn. There are 4 types of enemies Regular, Close-Combat, Sniper and Heavy. * = can be armoured, ie more durable
Regular* - The Grunts. SMG/Shotgunners/Assault Rifle all day, everyday. Shotgunners tend to charge at you which can be a danger
Close-Combat - Remember that Banzai Soldier from World at War? This is him except that its 1 hit kill, he dodges and insta-kills you with his knife when he gets close (Yes, no QTE)
Sniper* - He snipes? Also has shiny red laser sight which you can see since its tagging you
Heavy* - Always comes armoured and just like the Bulldozer from Payday 2, his face is his weakspot. There are 2 varieties of the 'Heavy', M249 Saw or AA12. Either way you're boned as they love walking straight up to you... Jerks

Don't worry about your AI though as they are okay-ish enough to get stuff done though they tend to go suicidal when you issue an attack order. They have no problem in getting kills or distracting enemies and will always shout out enemies of interest during a firefight such as, "Shotgunner coming from the right!". Take note that this needs to be heard as battle lines are not subtitled. What can be annoying though is when they take too much damamge, they need to be revived and you have a time limit but you don't have the ability to be revived (On Hard, idk about normal and easy)

(Core)
The meat of the game comes from being a Cover-Based Third Person Shooter reminiscent to that of games like Gears of War. Basically, you sprint form cover to cover (Using a Toggle Key 'Space') and rely on Regenerating Health. The lower your health, the more bloodied your screen becomes in addition to being Black and White (CoD anyone?). There are 15 weapons in total give or take which felt the same with only the diffference being its 'Alternate Function' key which is 'C'. There are also 3 grenade types, Frag, Sticky and Stun which are pretty self-explanatory. You can carry 2 weapons and all 3 grenade types at once. However, you are only limited to 3 grenades per type making the total number of grenades which can be carried to 9(3 Frags/3 Stickies/3 Stuns). Different from other games is how ammo is obtained here. While there is still the basic, 'pick up ammo from dead body so long as same weapon' concept, what Spec Ops has added to spice it up is that in this game is that you can actually Execute wounded enemies to get ammo for your current weapon type. Because you know.. Executions are fun. Be fast though or they'll bleed out to death(GoW anyone)

In a nutshell, it's your run of the mill Third Person Cover based shooter like Gears of War or Future Soldier.. Just like any other games where you're the unstoppable saviour of your country.

(Command)
As Leader, you have control of 2 Squad Mates who use order via the MMB. They are:
Lieutenant Adams
Your Heavy Weapons Specialist carrying the M249 Saw. Order him to attack an enemy so long as their close and he'll do two things. FIrst, he unleashes hell on them with suppressive fire from his weapon. Second, he throws a frag which finds its mark 90% of the time, the 10% due to the enemy running away from it

Sergeant Lugo
Your Sniper. Order him to attack an enemy from long range and he'll kill the guy so long as he has vision. Though it takes some time for him to pull the trigger, its usually a 1-shot kill

As you can see, the command aspect in this game is very weak but simple enough to make life easy.

(Environment)
Alongside your Red Explosive Containers, you also have the sand which can either help or hinder you. Firstly, Sand can act as either an alternative form of Explosive Barrels. Secondly, throwing an explosive into a pile of sand would create a sand cloud which effectively stuns all nearby enemies for a nice amount of time, similar to Stun grenades if I'm not mistaken. Later in the game at set stages, you'll come across Sandstorms which does two things. Making you unable to issue orders and increasing weapon spread. Extremely frustrating, especially on harder difficulties (15+ deaths on Hard)

Nothing revolutionary here really though I'll admit its interesting in theory.

(Misc)
Collectables are available in the game and are called Intels. The number of intels available in each level is shown by pressing Escape. It offers backstory to the world of Dubai and its inhabitants. As of the time this review was written, no Steam Trading Cards are available. Checkpoints in this game seem to be fair enough. 1 checkpoint pre and post engagement.
________________________________________________________________
Music and Sound

I like the music. It's nice... very Vietnam War-esque and is also perfectly timed and well-executed. It's either Gung Ho adrenaline fueled action or music that make you muse over your actions.

Sound also seems to be quite good though the sound of the AA12 doesn't seem to have too much force behind it. Other than that, the sound can of this game can really make firefights here intense, especially on higher difficulties.
________________________________________________________________
Graphics

It looks nice enough if you really care so much about it. It's able to capture the violence and carnage you unleash (Yay carnage and violence cause that's what every military shooter needs right!... right?)
________________________________________________________________
Mutiplayer
There are two types of Multiplayer here.
Co-Op
2 players, 4 levels. A bit of a challenge when communication between the two is lacking. Can be fun for the first few times though I believe that it will lose its charm as fast as you finish it
Competetive
4v4 PvP from what I heard though sadly the cream of this game comes from the SP hence why I never bothered to try it out.
________________________________________________________________
Overall

Story is honestly speaking the saving grace for this game. It's what made it so spectacular as the entire gameplay is bland, rehashed and has been done countless times though it can be argued that the very fact that it copies its gameplay from other Military Games is what makes this so good. This is because of how Spec Ops question our beliefs on said game. Must buy.

Everyone’s favourite game of 2012, [i]Spec Ops: The Line[/i] dangerously straddles the line between not getting a recommendation due to being an admittedly bad game by all standards of design and variation. The saving grace, which has been discussed countless times, is the gut-wrenching 180 that the narrative takes directly into [i]Apocalypse Now[/i] Territory. The story takes place in Dubai, jewel of the United Arab Emirates and now a horrifying wasteland having been all but wiped off the map by a sandstorm of biblical proportions. We play as Martin Walker (Nolan North, doing the most obviously ‘Nolan North’ of his many voices), captain of a small squad of Delta Force soldiers on a mission to confirm the presence of survivors in Dubai, either civilian or members of the 33rd Infantry Battalion, led by Colonel John Konrad (yes it’s a [i]Heart of Darkness[/i] parallel, we get it), who Walker furiously jerks off in the introductory cinematic. Twists and turns ensue, and Delta Force ends up travelling throughout the city, growing more and more rife with infighting and unease as a variety of horrors turn them from a plucky band of would-be heroes into a traumatised pack of murderers. That’s one thing [i]Spec Ops[/i] does really well - deconstructing the concept of heroes and villains by setting up a proper evil maniac only to have him either die unceremoniously with no payoff or turn out to have not been the antagonist you expect, and even come to desire by the end. The game knows having a clear moral bad guy makes things more straightforward, and plays with this and many other audience expectations throughout the trail of guts and gore that is its story.

Like everybody else who first played [i]Spec Ops[/i] more than a week after release, I went in expecting to witness some pretty horrific stuff, but what I didn’t expect was just how introspective it gets. I went in with prior knowledge of the infamous ‘white phosphorous’ debacle, but the big fuss led me to expect that to be the worst of it, which made it even more uncomfortable when it wasn’t by a long shot. White phosphorous - which was a fake moral choice at best (you can’t progress without using it) - looks tame compared to later setpieces which give you an actual choice over whether or not to commit atrocities, but only after forcing you into a position where sometimes gunning down dozens of civilians or taking your loaded revolver and leaving a dying soldier to burn alive don’t seem like terrible ideas. It plays with your emotions, invokes feelings of rage and hate, and then makes you choose without giving those feelings time to wear off. One of the most effective devices is the way choices matter, which is to say that strictly speaking, they don’t. All of [i]Spec Ops[/i]’ multiple endings are left open right up until the end. Whether you choose to do awful, terrible things only affects your own perception of yourself as a player and Walker as a character - after the WP incident early on, it stops feeling like the characters in [i]Spec Ops[/i] are turning Walker into a creature more monster than man and starts feeling like [i]Spec Ops[/i] is turning you, the player into that creature.

It’s not fucking fun. At times things got confronting enough to make me feel physically ill, and at no point did I enjoy myself, because the gameplay is too bland to be fun even if I could bring yourself to somehow look past the things happening and go back to playing a computer game for entertainment. And if [i]Spec Ops[/i] was fun, it would totally undermine the message, which is not only that war is bad and makes good people into bad people, but also that everything you (and Walker) do, is pointless. Awful, sickening things happen regardless of whether you choose to take a direct hand in them. Similarly, regardless of what anyone writes or reads about [i]Spec Ops: The Line[/i], it’s a fucking masterwork of interactive storytelling that fully utilises and bends the framework of the very medium to tell the darkest, most confronting story to come out of video games to date.

I have to be honest, this game got to me, got inside my head and made me feel things I didn't think a basic, cliché, third person shooter could. There are plenty of games that show you violence, plenty of games have you run through all sorts of firefights and battles that are visually stunning making you feel awesome. You walk away from most firefights in this game feeling many feelings; sadness, guilt, horror and sickness. You start the game as a strapping commander of a small team of Special Forces, the serious "Captain America" type and sarcastic joker. You are entering the city of Dubai, struck by devastating dust storms trapping the 33rd and all the civilians they were trying to evacuate and of course, you know the CO of that unit, he was a good man who helped you in a past theater of war. All very, run of the mill story of a canned modern shooter. This is remarkably misleading. As you work your way through the city you find that order has utterly collapsed, you help soldiers under fire from apparent insurgents and as you go farther, you find American soldiers rounding up and gunning down civilians. You are forced to defend yourself when the turn their fire on you. It tears your team up and it is simply the beginning. The game constantly confronts you with choices between one evil or another. No one is the good guy, each side commits atrocities against each other, and if you hope to survive, you have to do the same. There are literally a pair of achievements named "Damned if you do" and "Damned if you don't". The game drags you through the mud watching soldiers, civilians and even your own team die. Your character's dialogue slowly devolves from in control tactical commands to screaming obscenities at the enemy and eventual hallucinations. This game brings themes from Apocalypse Now and The Heart of Darkness into the gaming world and confronts us with the true horrors of this level of violence. You don't walk away from this game feeling good about playing it, the game even goes meta, insinuating that you caused this violence; you could have shut it down and walked away at any time, why did you keep going? They are questions that demand answers. It is a game I think all gamers should play; it rocks you, makes you feel uneasy and forces you to appreciate the true nature of violence. The gameplay itself is smooth and user friendly. Basic squad commands and different guns give you multiple approaches to different combat scenarios. The gameplay is linear and simply escalated as different guns and enemies are introduced with smarter AI and better fighters, much like most of the Call of Duty franchise, although this game, I enjoyed more. Overall, this game is deeply dark and challenges you to confront its own violence. I believe that anyone who plays shooters should play this game to remind them how horrific true violence is; there is nothing wrong with playing our video games that are violent, we just can't become numb to it and this game keeps us grounded.

It's tempting to give The Line a thumbs down, given that I did not have a good time and it seriously bummed me out. But the thing is, that's pretty much the point of the game. Ever watched Platoon and thought "damn, I wish that was me"? Well, maybe find a good psychiatrist, but also definitely try Spec Ops: The Line because it will scratch that itch without the considerable distress of having to be Charlie Sheen.

So while it initially seems to be yet another piece of Modern Warfare-style hooah military porn, it doesn't take long for a metaphorical nun to enter the room and punish you for vigorously exercising your assault rifle. (That's a metaphor we can all relate to, right? No, just me? Alrighty then.) Turns out The Line is more about the horrors of war than the thrill of whipping out your beefy gleaming weapon in front of a bunch of guys.

[h1]But seriously...[/h1]
Pretend I'm narrating the rest of this review in Al Gore's voice, because from here on out it's super serious. The set-up is that Dubai has been partially evacuated before an apocalyptic sandstorm, leaving the remaining population isolated and starving. A US army battalion disobeys orders and stays in the city to look after its residents, but as supplies dwindle, the colonel institutes martial law and starts executing civilians. You play a Delta Force operative sent in to investigate the city's comms blackout and renegade battalion. You arrive to find a hellscape of bodies, fire, ruination and blinding sand.

And that's the happiest part, before your actions descend the Delta Force team into a pit of trauma and moral degradation. I won't throw any spoilers in here, but The Line forces you to do some pretty horrendous things that made me feel sick. You're usually given some degree of choice, but only enough to feel even worse about it. There's also the fact that the enemies you're gunning down in droves aren't invading aliens, demons, mad cultists or endangered wildlife poachers, they're American soldiers who tried to do the right thing and ended up stuck in the moral pit that you're teetering over. While the shooting dynamic is fine (third-person cover-intensive linear shooter - think Call of Duty crossed with Gears of War), you can never wholly enjoy it because of who you're fighting. In fact, it's often hard to tell if it's your enemies talking or your squadmates.

Like Apocalypse Now, it's loosely inspired by Joseph Conrad's novella Heart of Darkness, and has that film's sense of surreal horror too. It's more like Platoon in terms of the feeling you get, and the way camaraderie can give way to hate. The campaign is short, less than five hours, but the choices you can make along the way add a little variety to things, including a Mass Effect-style final level that allows several different endings (four according to Wikipedia). There's multiplayer and co-op, but given that the game has been out for a while, those are best sampled with friends rather than waiting to hook up with a rando.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Feels bad, man, but it's a unique game that aspires to emulate some of cinema's most powerful projects. I'd much rather hide behind the level of dissociation you get from watching this sort of thing in a movie, but if you [i]really[/i] want to feel that horror on a personal level, here's your game.

[h1]“Do you feel like a hero yet?”[/h1]
While organizing my steam library recently, I randomly came across this game that had apparently been delisted. Before this, I had never looked into this title in any serious depth, but since I somehow owned it and it was no longer available for purchase, I became curious and decided to give it a try. To my surprise, it completely blew me away.

It starts off like a standard military shooter, but if you keep playing for another hour or two, you’ll start to realize that something isn't quite right. Walker, the protagonist, initially appears to be the typical American soldier - who is brave, calm, and willing to complete the mission. However, as the story progresses, players slowly begin to realize that this operation is far more complicated than it first appeared, and Walker and his squad are gradually losing the things they once believed in.

Although the game’s anti-war message is incredibly deep, it never sacrifices the gameplay experience and it definitely does not turn itself into a boring or miserable TPS just to deliver its message. Mechanically, the gameplay is not particularly innovative, it borrowed the cover-based shooting from Gears series, which was pretty common in those TPS on Xbox 360 at the time. Throughout the game, [b]you constantly move from cover to cover, pop off a few shots, and then push forward to the next position[/b]. However, because the developers polished this core gameplay loop quite well - and because this style of shooter has become much less common nowadays - it is still surprisingly enjoyable to play in 2026. The game also features a squad command mechanic, but compared to something like Mass Effect, it lacks any real depth and feels more like a minor gimmick.

The story takes inspiration from Heart of Darkness, and I have to say, it successfully recreates the novel’s theme of how human psychology changes under extreme circumstances. I don’t want to spoil the story, but I can say that many of the things you do throughout the game seem completely justified on the surface because you are simply trying to complete your mission. However, as the story unfolds, you slowly begin to realize that things are not what you originally thought they were.

The strength of this narrative structure is that all the small hints and buildup from earlier chapters eventually come together and explode in Chapter 15, making the final twist [b]extremely impactful[/b]. But the weakness is that players never truly have control over Walker’s decisions. No matter how much the story criticizes war, you are still forced to pick up your weapon, keep shooting enemies, and continue making the same mistakes over and over again (though honestly that is kind of realistic).

Beyond the story, the game’s environmental design is also outstanding. A Dubai swallowed by sandstorms is an incredibly unique setting, and we get to see a city that once represented wealth and prosperity has now become a desolate wasteland in this game. Honestly, I don’t even know how to properly describe this aesthetic, but I absolutely love it.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3783708583
The sand is not just a visual decoration either, sometimes you have to fight enemies in the middle of massive sandstorms, and other times you can strategically break glass at the right angle to release waves of sand and bury your enemies. These details constantly strengthen the game's atmosphere and immersion.

It is also worth mentioning that the developers hid many small details and secrets throughout the game, using Walker’s mental state to create a narrative where reality and illusion constantly blur together. ([spoiler]for example, the choices you make during Riggs’ ending can affect the graffiti and sculptures you encounter later[/spoiler]). Although most of the hallucinations are explained by Chapter 15, there are still some subtle details that are easy to miss. You can check out this Story Explanation and Analysis video if you are interested: [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tULRgsc362o][/url]

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3784015768
If you look at it purely as a shooter, Spec Ops: The Line is far from a perfect game. Its gameplay is not particularly inspired, the visuals are not what you would consider outstanding, and the controls can feel somewhat awkward. Nevertheless, the point of Spec Ops: The Line was never to provide a satisfying power fantasy through shooting. Throughout the entire experience, whether through other characters’ dialogue or the quotes shown during loading screens, the word “hero” appears again and again, the game constantly forces you to confront one uncomfortable question:

[b]“Do you feel like a hero yet?”[/b]

These moments remind you that this is not just another shallow military shooter built around glorifying heroism. Instead, it uses one of the genres most responsible for romanticizing war to challenge the player’s understanding of violence, heroism, and the consequences of war itself.

TL;DR: The Line played on FUBAR difficulty in one continuous playthrough is the best recreation of combat you'll find in any medium. It took me roughly 14 hours to get through, dying often and trying the same section repeatedly.

Full review (warning possible spoilers):

The effect of playing The Line on FUBAR in one sitting was revelatory. The Line does what video games do at their best: give us the experience of being somewhere and doing something without actually being there. In my playthrough controlling Captain Walker I spent many long, agonising, frustrating, exhausting hours getting him through one combat situation to the next.

I screamed, pounded my desk, and lost my sh**. The designers even sync the points in the game where both the player and Walker start losing it simultaneously. The controls are janky and even after multiple playthroughs I still found myself accidentally shifting Walker out of cover and killing him. Other times I'd be prompting Walker to swap his weapon instead of reloading in the middle of an intense firefight. 

The effect is that the gameplay elements compliment the meta theme underlying The Line's writing. The player becomes alienated from Walker as he apparently no longer responds to our input. The slip ups caused by the control scheme seem intentional; they mimic the way the human body starts failing to react the way we want it to after prolonged exposure to stress.

Moreover, the player's growing frustration with the sqaud mechanics mirrors Walker's own frustration with his men. You begin to berate them just as Walker does for perceived failings. Nolan North, Christopher Reid, and Omid Abtahi who voice Cpt. Martin Walker, Lt. Alphonso Adams, and Sgt. John Lugo respectively, do an impressive job of capturing the disintegration of Delta Force.

Each man ends up resenting one another - military discipline deteriorates and the squad is barely a unit in the latter stages of the game. The further you go in the game the further morale stretches and then fails. Neither the player or Walker is enjoying themselves, both are just looking forward to the next respite or the end around the corner.

As for the enemy in the Line, whether refugees or 33rd, their novelty wears off real fast. Soon you take glee in having Walker kill them, even execute them when they're incapacitated and no longer a threat.

On a continuous playthrough you sympathise with Walker to a much greater degree. Neither you nor he has had a break, and consequently both your decisions stop making much sense. I died a lot through my single playthrough, and after a while you start making mistakes with increasing frequency. I even started accidentally shooting my own squad members because they look so much like the 33rd. Fog of war indeed.

The end result is that you're worn by the last chapter. Your nerves are shot. At the end you - like Walker - are apathetic. He even throws down his weapon in the closing showdown with the 33rd, much to the incredulity and fury of Adams.

There are plenty of shooters that let you feel like a hero. Spec Ops: The Line asks a much more uncomfortable question: what if you aren't one?

The gameplay is intentionally familiar. It starts as another military shooter, making you believe you know exactly where the story is going. Then, little by little, it tears apart every expectation the genre has built over the years. Instead of celebrating violence, it forces you to confront it.

The real masterpiece is the story. Without spoiling anything, Spec Ops: The Line isn't about winning a war—it's about how easily good intentions can spiral into catastrophe. It explores guilt, trauma, pride, and the way people justify increasingly horrific actions when convinced they're doing the right thing. By the end, you're left questioning not just the characters' decisions, but your own role as the player.

What makes the narrative so powerful is that it doesn't exist in a vacuum. Throughout history, military interventions have often begun with promises of liberation, security, or peace, only to descend into prolonged conflict and immense human suffering. Whether you think of Vietnam, Iraq, Afghanistan, or countless other wars, the game captures the uncomfortable reality that the line between hero and villain is often blurred by perspective, propaganda, and the consequences of decisions made under pressure. It doesn't offer easy answers—it asks difficult questions.

Perhaps that's why Spec Ops: The Line remains one of gaming's most important stories. It refuses to glorify war. Instead, it examines the psychological and moral cost of it, making it one of the few games that treats its audience like adults.

It's genuinely heartbreaking that this game has been delisted due to licensing issues. A title this influential deserves to be preserved and made available to future generations. More than a decade later, its themes remain just as relevant, if not more so.

This isn't just one of the best stories in gaming—it's one of the few that genuinely has something meaningful to say.

This might be one of the few shooter games where killing an enemy puts me at unease.

You play as Martin Walker, commander of Delta Forces, who is on Dubai trying to evacuate the civilians from sandstorm. The 33rd Divison went there first, but never returned, so it is up to you to continue their task... or not.

I mispredicted the game would take the usual cliche "rescue mission gone awry because someone screwed it up" - but I was wrong, completely wrong..

With its gripping storytelling, the game it delves to the traumas of war, the ambiguousness of war (that war isn't black and white), and. most importantly, how accustomed we are in murdering faceless people as entertainment. The game started with the usual heroic "we're going to save the day, lads" pro-war stance shooter games usually have, but as you progress, it turned its head to portray how terrible trying to act as an hero can be.

I also like the minor details. In every cutscenes, you're given options how to deal with conflicts presented. E.g., should you rescue the civilians or an agent? Should you shoot the enemy or let them talk first? Should you shoot that guy, this guy, or... abandon order at all?

The consequence doesn't have major effect, but it opens up different reaction and dialogues. Even the smallest ones like standing in front of your teammates while they are ziplining. The environment is also rich in details: barricades are destructible, bullet goes through clothes, etc; sometimes giving you different tactics to progress through the levels.

The cons of this game - well, the covering system sometimes doesn't really work well. So sometimes it's kinda difficult to move from one cover to another. But mostly it's not really a problem. Also, the game punish you for running and gunning; it's more tactical shooter like, so if you're coming from Call of Duty or the like, you would need to adapt.

This game has one of the most intense and gripping story I've played since long; I'd say it's fitting to say this game as a war thriller movie bundled as a third person shooter. The game deserves an award for its mind-blowing narrative.

It leaves you feeling worse after playing than before—and that is its greatest achievement.

Verdict: Spec Ops: The Line is the most emotionally taxing shooter I have ever played. It shows the true, ugly face of war.

Spec Ops the line is a loose adaption of Heart of Darkness/Apocalypse Now that masks itself as a typical tactical military third person shooter, but is really more like a surrealist psychological/horror/thriller. It is a relatively short (about 4-5 hour) game about a Delta Force team that is sent into Dubai 6 months after a natural disaster cut it off from the world. The overall gameplay of the title is a typical third person shooter with very very light tactical options and clunky mechanics that do not really distinguish it from other titles of the genre during that time period. 

What the game does stand out for is its mind bending and surrealist plot that heavily deconstructs the military shooter genre with a meta commentary about why would someone want to play a game where you just kill scores of people without a thought to the moral consequences while believing you are the hero. You will either come out of this thinking it was a very bold artistic decision that excellently gets its point across and is thought provoking enough to really make you think about the moral ramifications of enjoying violent videogames. Or you will think that it is a hypocritical pretentious critic bait that tells you that you are a garbage person for playing this game and enjoying it and you would be better off turning it off and going outside. 

As a whole I believe that Spec Ops: The Line is worth checking out when it is on sale for $5.00. It is a short title that offers a thought provoking and surreal story with a beautiful setting and haunting visuals. The gameplay is not anything to write home about but the story might be something that sticks with you and make you ponder it years later.

First things first, *NO SPOILERS*. I get this game during the Christmas sale last year, but I never get the chance, or the will, to install and play it. Friends have told me it was a game I have to tried, in which I felt a bit unnerved since I have also hear the 'notorious' reputation this game has. Now that I have installed and played it to the end, I am not sure what to feel.....

Spec Ops: The Line is an old game (since I can run it on very high with my potato). On first glance, its main theme centers on shooting, and war. While it is played with 3rd person view, people will group it with other 3rd person view titles, such as Tom Clancy, or the other, more famous AAA titles, like Battlefield and Call of Duty franchises. In general, they have similar game modes i.e. multiplayer, in-game mechanics (although the latter titles are first-person shooters) i.e. vaulting over cover, melee attacks. Nonetheless, I had planned this game to be finished quick, and move on. I was wrong. The game-for some reason-from the moment I start playing it, I can't stop.The only time I stopped, it was to eat dinner, and sleep. Even then, I can't stop thinking about it. D:

The game starts in an aerial fight scene, helicopters buzzing around, shooting other helis down using minigun. Sounds familiar? For people who have played other similar themed games, you would know what I mean. Then, the sandstorm comes in. *̶c̶u̶e̶s̶ ̶f̶o̶r̶ ̶t̶h̶e̶ ̶d̶a̶r̶u̶d̶e̶ ̶-̶ ̶s̶a̶n̶d̶s̶t̶o̶r̶m̶ ̶s̶o̶n̶g̶ ̶a̶n̶d̶ ̶m̶e̶m̶e̶s̶ ̶i̶n̶c̶o̶m̶i̶n̶g̶*̶  Then, a crash.

Then, the game starts. In a desert, one plays as the main character, Captain Walker. Accompanied by his two subordinates, Sergeant Lugo and Lieutenant Adams to Dubai, trying to find Colonel Konrad and the 33rd Batalyon along with survivors. This 'search for survivors' does sound like an over-used plot device utilized by so many game companies, I had consider it to be the most basic 'norm' developers use to start any similar themed games. However, after the first few chapters where I somewhat understands the basic gameplay (cover and shoot, give orders, etc.) I did think that this is similar to Tom Clancy's franchises. However, as the game goes deeper, I start to understand why the game had the reputation which sets itself apart from other titles. The actions; words that the MC, Lugo and Adams used; enemy executions (Yes, there is an option for that); their clothes and wellbeing; the words on screen that appear when you die and restart from the last checkpoint; even the early game backgrounds when the game starts up, REALLY CHANGE as the game goes on. I start to question, what was going on.

Then, at one point, one scene was particularly... unsettling. It was one of that 'What did I just do" moments. Through out the game, I was presented with choices that I have to make in a limited time. However, there are multiple times when one is presented with choices where choosing either of them will lead to bad situations.  In this type of moments, one usually chooses the one which is the lesser evil. Still, how do one knows that the choice IS the lesser evil? At that moment, no one knows. Only later on in the game, one finds out and it is not a pretty one. 

The later stages in the game are a bit frustrating since I failed and died a few times (which even prompted the 'do you want to lower the difficulty' sign). I have to remap the controls since vaulting over cover and melee attack are mapped originally at the same key, which made it difficult. Ammos are also limited, forcing you to drop and switch weapons to deal with certain situations i.e. snipers, juggernauts. Movements are a bit mechanical (which caused several deaths) but I put it down to my ability since I was not accustomized to the playstyle. I have to give props for the AI enemy who are particularly challenging (even on normal difficulty that I was playing) which will force you to get out of your cover by throwing grenades, flanking you and will kill you when they had the chance i̶n̶ ̶t̶h̶e̶ ̶m̶i̶d̶s̶t̶ ̶o̶f̶ ̶r̶o̶c̶k̶ ̶m̶u̶s̶i̶c̶ ̶b̶l̶a̶r̶i̶n̶g̶ ̶o̶v̶e̶r̶ ̶t̶h̶e̶ ̶s̶p̶e̶a̶k̶e̶r̶s̶ ̶a̶s̶ ̶b̶u̶l̶l̶e̶t̶s̶ ̶w̶h̶i̶z̶z̶e̶d̶ ̶p̶a̶s̶t̶ ̶b̶y̶ ̶a̶n̶d̶ ̶g̶r̶e̶n̶a̶d̶e̶s̶ ̶c̶a̶u̶s̶i̶n̶g̶ ̶a̶ ̶m̶o̶m̶e̶n̶t̶a̶r̶y̶ ̶s̶t̶u̶n̶. AI friendlies are surprisingly useful, helping during tough battle scenes, even though sometimes they went down because they just stand there while the enemy shoots at them. :/

Into the 5th or 6th hour, in my mind, I started to think how does this game end? How? Who is Konrad? The earlier chapters I have played is already.... confronting enough. And then I played the last few chapters. Watching everything I hold dear, MC, the other guys, break and fall. Sometimes I don't even know if these guys could've reach this far, considering what they went through. Then, the final chapter, and epilogue came. It was... an emotional rollercoaster. For the first time when I play a game, as the credits roll, I tried to gain some understanding on what had happened up there. For the first time, when I played games of such genre, I feel... mainly upset. However, to call it just upset is not exactly correct.  Of course,  I feel upset that I had played this game, as one starts the game thinking of what was the general norm in such games, and in the end... felt empty inside. There is also a combination of conflicting and mixed feelings of confusion, and relief. Why I put relief? Because, I get the chance to play this game. It was one of those games where you just have to experience it once, without spoilers, and knowing nothing about the game at all. 

I have been particularly late in playing games that are not popular anymore but people still consider it timeless. It has been the case for a few games I own i.e. Bioshock, Bioshock 2, Bioshock Infinite, and Walking Dead: Season 1. I was glad, I had the chance to try a game that invoked such conflicting emotions and thoughts, even after the game have ended.
